intro: Southeast Asia is home to many martial arts with long histories. In Thailand, boxing grew from temple fairs and royal events into a ring sport with stadiums, gloves and a national law. Across the Malay world, silat is a large family of arts shown at weddings and in scored matches. In the Philippines, arnis became the national martial art by law in 2009.

These arts also traveled. Filipino farm workers taught eskrima in California backyards. Indo families brought pencak silat to the Netherlands. Thai boxing camps now welcome students from around the world, and a bundle of arnis sticks can sit in a Chicago school closet. Each move brought new rooms, new rules and new questions about names.

In this unit you will read about objects like the mongkon and the pra jiad, and about bodies like IPSI, PERSILAT, IFMA and WEKAF. You will compare legends with records. By the end, you will be able to explain how an art can live in a stadium, a village and a school gym at the same time.
bigQuestion: How do martial arts from Southeast Asia keep their meaning when they move into stadiums, federations and gyms far from home?

title: Southeast Asia and Travel

chapters.title: Muay Thai Objects
chapters.bigQuestion: How did Thailand's ring sport grow from older boxing, and what do its objects tell us about the people who keep it?

story.title: A Hoop, an Armband, a Ring Plan
story.kicker: Two small objects on a paper plan open a long history of Thai boxing.
paragraphs: A seventh-grade class in Chicago visits a small museum show about Thailand. In one glass case lies a printed plan of a boxing ring. It is a square with four corner posts and ropes. A circle of rope wrapped in cloth rests on top of the plan. Beside it lies a thin band of cloth, tied in a knot.

A card names the objects. The circle is a mongkon, a head hoop. The band is a pra jiad, an armband. Both come from a Muay Thai gym in Thailand. The card says a teacher gave them to a boxer. They were not bought in a store.

A student named Mali leans closer. Her grandmother grew up in Bangkok. "My grandma says you do not put a mongkon on the floor," she tells the class. The museum guide nods. She explains that many Thai gyms treat the head hoop with great care.

The guide points to a timeline on the wall. It starts long before rings and ropes. It shows boxing at temple fairs and royal events in old Siam. Then it shows the first Bangkok stadiums in the 1940s and 1950s. At the end, it shows the International Olympic Committee fully recognizing Muay Thai's world federation in 2021.

"So the ring plan is new," says Mali. "But the hoop is older." The guide smiles. "Both are part of the story," she says. "The ring came from new rules. The hoop came from teachers and their students."
story.think: Why might a gym object mean something different in a museum case than in a costume shop?

lessons.title: Many Styles Before One Name
lessons.mainIdea: Before modern Muay Thai, many regions of Siam had their own boxing styles, now often grouped as muay boran.
reading: The Thai word *muay* means boxing. Long before stadiums, people in Siam boxed at temple fairs, festivals and royal events. Siam was the old name of the kingdom. The government changed the country's name to Thailand in 1939.

Boxing was not the same everywhere. Thai histories name regional styles from places like Chaiya in the south, Korat in the northeast and Lopburi in the center. Each region had its own teachers and its own habits. Today people often group these older styles under one name, *muay boran*, which means ancient boxing.

Muay boran is a modern label for many older practices. It is not one single school. Some gyms today teach muay boran as a separate art, apart from the ring sport. Historians say the regional styles fed into the ring sport of the 1900s.

words.d: the Thai word for boxing
"ancient boxing"; a modern name for the older regional boxing styles of Siam
the old name of the kingdom of Thailand, used until 1939

look.title: Three Places, One Word

lessons.title: The Story of Nai Khanom Tom
lessons.mainIdea: Thai tradition tells of a captured boxer, Nai Khanom Tom, and the story is honored today, though historians treat it as a legend.
reading: In 1767, an army from Burma captured and destroyed Ayutthaya. Ayutthaya was the capital of Siam at that time. Many people from the city were taken to Burma as prisoners. This part of the history is well documented.

A later Thai story tells of one prisoner, *Nai Khanom Tom*. In the story, a Burmese king held a festival. He asked a Siamese boxer to face Burmese fighters. Nai Khanom Tom won match after match. The king then set him free.

Historians call this story a *legend*. It comes from later writings, not from records made at the time. Still, it matters a great deal in Thailand. Many gyms tell the story to new students. Thailand marks National Muay Thai Day on March 17 in his honor.

words.d: a Siamese boxer in a Thai legend set after the fall of Ayutthaya in 1767
a story passed down about the past that historians cannot fully confirm
the capital of Siam until an army from Burma destroyed it in 1767

look.prompt: Which column is documented history, and which is a legend? How can you tell?

lessons.title: Royal Fairs and Champions
lessons.mainIdea: Kings of Siam watched and sponsored boxing, and King Chulalongkorn honored champion boxers from the provinces.
reading: Boxing in Siam was close to the royal court. Kings watched matches at fairs and ceremonies. Some kings kept skilled boxers in royal service. Chronicles also tell stories of kings who boxed themselves, but those accounts mix history and legend.

King *Chulalongkorn*, also called Rama V, ruled Siam from 1868 to 1910. Thai histories say he held boxing events and gave royal titles to champion boxers from several provinces. A royal title was a rank of honor from the king. It raised the boxer's standing at home.

These royal events brought boxers from different regions to one place. Teachers from Chaiya, Korat and Lopburi could see one another's styles. Historians see this mixing as one step toward a shared national ring sport.

words.d: King Rama V of Siam, who ruled from 1868 to 1910
a rank of honor given by the king

look.prompt: How could an event like this help different regional styles become one sport?

lessons.title: From Rope Bindings to Gloves
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1920s and 1930s, Thai boxing moved into roped rings with timed rounds, and gloves replaced rope-bound hands.
reading: For a long time, Thai boxers wrapped their hands with cords of hemp or cotton. Matches were often held on open ground, with the crowd forming the edge. There were no fixed weight classes. Rules could change from place to place.

In the 1920s, Bangkok began to hold matches in a square *ring* with ropes, like Western boxing. The ring gave the match a clear edge. Timed rounds and a referee came into use. Western boxing was already popular in Bangkok, and its rules offered a model.

By the 1930s, *gloves* had replaced rope bindings in Bangkok matches. Thai accounts link this change to worries about serious injuries. Weight classes followed. The result was a new ring sport. People began to call it Muay Thai, meaning Thai boxing, to set it apart from Western boxing, called muay sakon.

words.d: a square area with corner posts and ropes where a boxing match is held
padded coverings for the hands that replaced rope bindings in Thai boxing by the 1930s
the Thai name for international, Western-style boxing

lessons.title: Two Great Stadiums
lessons.mainIdea: Rajadamnern Stadium (1945) and Lumpinee Stadium (1956) made Bangkok the center of professional Muay Thai.
reading: A *stadium* is a large building made for watching sports. Bangkok's first great Muay Thai stadium is Rajadamnern. Work on it began under Prime Minister Plaek Phibunsongkhram. It opened in 1945, just after World War II.

*Lumpinee* Stadium opened in 1956. The Royal Thai Army runs it. For decades it stood on Rama IV Road in central Bangkok. In 2014 it moved to a new building in the Ram Inthra area in the north of the city.

The two stadiums set the standard for the sport. A title belt from Rajadamnern or Lumpinee became one of the highest honors a Thai boxer could win. Boxers from gyms all over Thailand travel to Bangkok hoping to fight there. Their rankings and champions are followed across the country.

words.d: a large building made for watching sports
a Bangkok Muay Thai stadium that opened in 1945
a Bangkok Muay Thai stadium run by the Royal Thai Army; it opened in 1956 and moved in 2014

lessons.title: Rounds, Music and the Law
lessons.mainIdea: A professional match has five three-minute rounds, and Thailand's Boxing Act of 1999 set rules for professional boxing.
reading: A professional Muay Thai match in Thailand has five *rounds*. Each round lasts three minutes. Boxers rest for two minutes between rounds. Judges score each round, and a referee runs the match in the ring.

Live music plays during a match. People often call this music *sarama*, after its best-known tune. A small band plays it on a Java pipe, a wind instrument called pi chawa, with two drums and small cymbals called ching. The music speeds up as a round goes on. The band is part of the event, not a background recording.

In 1999, Thailand passed the *Boxing Act*. The law set up a national committee for professional boxing. It required boxers, gyms and promoters to register. A promoter is the person or company that organizes and sells a match. The law applies to both Muay Thai and Western boxing in Thailand.

the best-known tune of the live music played during a Muay Thai match; people often use it as a name for that music

a person or company that organizes and sells a match

check.q: What did Thailand's Boxing Act of 1999 do?

lessons.title: The Mongkon Head Hoop
lessons.mainIdea: The mongkon is a head hoop a teacher gives to a boxer; many gyms treat it as a sign of the bond between teacher and student.
reading: A *mongkon* is a hoop worn on the head. It is often made of rope wound with cloth. In many Thai gyms, the teacher gives the mongkon to a boxer. Some gyms hold a small ceremony when a student first receives one.

On fight night, the boxer wears the mongkon into the ring. In many gyms, the teacher or trainer takes it off the boxer's head before the first round. Some trainers say a short blessing as they do. The boxer does not fight with it on.

Many gyms keep strict customs about the mongkon. It is hung up high, not set on the floor or stepped over. It belongs to the gym as much as to the boxer. Because of this, many Thai teachers dislike seeing a mongkon sold as a party costume. To them, it is a sign of the *teacher* and student bond.

words.d: a head hoop that a Muay Thai teacher gives a boxer; worn into the ring and removed before the fight
in Muay Thai, the kru, who trains boxers and gives them gym marks such as the mongkon

look.title: Two Hoops

look.prompt: The two hoops may look alike. How is their meaning different, and why might a gym care?

check.why: In many Thai gyms, the teacher gives the mongkon to a boxer.

check.q: When is the mongkon taken off on fight night?

lessons.title: The Pra Jiad Armband
lessons.mainIdea: The pra jiad is a cloth armband worn on the upper arm; unlike the mongkon, many boxers keep it on during the fight.
reading: A *pra jiad* is a band of cloth tied around the upper arm. A boxer may wear one on one arm or on both arms. Unlike the mongkon, the pra jiad often stays on during the match. Its colors and knots vary from gym to gym.

A popular story explains where the pra jiad came from. In the story, young men going off to war tied on a strip of cloth from their mother's clothing for protection. Historians cannot confirm this story. It is best treated as a *tradition* that families and gyms tell.

Today many gyms give out armbands of different colors. Some international groups use colored armbands to show a student's level, a bit like colored belts in judo. That system is recent. In older Thai gyms, the pra jiad was a personal gift, not a rank.

words.d: a cloth armband worn on the upper arm by Muay Thai boxers
a custom or belief handed down over time within a group

lessons.title: The Wai Kru Before a Match
lessons.mainIdea: Before a match, boxers perform the wai kru ram muay, a ceremony that honors their teachers.
reading: Before a match, each boxer performs the *wai kru ram muay*. The Thai word wai means a gesture of respect with palms pressed together. Kru means teacher. The whole name means paying respect to the teacher with a boxing dance.

The ceremony happens in the ring, with the band playing. Each boxer moves slowly around the ring. Many gyms have their own version, passed from teacher to student. A person who knows the sport can sometimes tell which gym a boxer comes from by watching.

In many gyms, the wai kru honors teachers, parents and the gym's line of teachers. Some boxers also think of the Buddha or of their home region. The meaning can differ from gym to gym. What stays the same is that it happens before the first round, while the boxer still wears the mongkon.

words.d: the ceremony before a Muay Thai match that honors a boxer's teachers
a Thai gesture of respect made with the palms pressed together
the Thai word for teacher

look.title: Order of the Evening
look.text: At a Bangkok stadium the night runs in order: the boxers enter wearing the mongkon; the band begins to play; each boxer performs the wai kru; the trainers remove the mongkon; the bell rings for round one.
look.prompt: Why might the wai kru come before the mongkon is removed, and not after?

check.why: The wai kru ram muay is a ceremony that honors a boxer's teachers.

lessons.title: Camp Names in the Ring
lessons.mainIdea: Thai boxers often fight under a ring name that includes the name of their gym, so the camp travels with them.
reading: A Muay Thai gym in Thailand is often called a *camp*. In Thai it is khai muay. Many young boxers live at the camp. They train there, eat there and travel from there to matches. Some camps are family businesses run by a former boxer.

Many boxers fight under a *ring name*. The ring name often joins the boxer's first name to the camp's name. For example, the boxer later known as Buakaw Banchamek first became famous as Buakaw Por. Pramuk. Por. Pramuk was the name of his gym. When the boxer wins, the camp's name is announced too.

Some Thai boxers moved between Muay Thai and Western boxing. Samart Payakaroon was a Muay Thai star at Lumpinee in the early 1980s. In 1986 he won a world title in Western boxing from the World Boxing Council. His career shows how the two ring sports stood side by side in Thailand.

words.d: a Muay Thai gym in Thailand, where many boxers live and train; in Thai, khai muay
the name a boxer fights under, often joined to the gym's name

look.title: Reading a Poster
look.text: A fight poster from Bangkok lists two boxers. Each name has two parts. The second part is the same as the name painted over the door of a gym in a northeastern province.
look.prompt: What does the second part of each name tell you about where the boxer comes from?

choices: a Muay Thai camp or gym
check.why: Khai muay is the Thai name for a Muay Thai camp, where many boxers live and train.

check.q: Where did the Por. Pramuk part of Buakaw's early ring name come from?
check.why: Por. Pramuk was the name of his gym, joined to his first name as a ring name.

lessons.title: Neighbors With Their Own Names
lessons.mainIdea: Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos each have their own ring sports, and the question of names has sometimes caused disputes.
reading: Thailand's neighbors have their own boxing traditions. In Myanmar, the ring sport is *lethwei*. It is known for being fought without padded gloves. In Laos, people practice muay Lao. In Cambodia, the ring sport has long been called pradal serey.

These arts share a long border history. Kingdoms in the region traded, fought and moved people for centuries. So they share some customs, such as live music and a ceremony before a match. Each country tells its own history of its sport, and each is proud of it.

Names can become a public dispute. In 2023, Cambodia hosted the Southeast Asian Games. It listed the ring sport under the name *Kun Khmer*, not muay. Thailand's team did not enter those events. The dispute showed that a sport's name can carry national pride.

words.d: the traditional ring sport of Myanmar, known for being fought without padded gloves
the name Cambodia uses for its ring sport, long called pradal serey
a multi-sport event for countries of Southeast Asia, first held in Bangkok in 1959

look.title: Four Countries, Four Names
look.text: Thailand: Muay Thai. Myanmar: lethwei. Laos: muay Lao. Cambodia: pradal serey, now also called Kun Khmer. Each sport has a ring, a crowd and a history its people are proud of.
look.prompt: Why might a country care about which name is used for its ring sport at an international event?

check.why: Lethwei is the traditional ring sport of Myanmar.

check.q: What name did Cambodia use for its ring sport at the 2023 Southeast Asian Games?
check.why: Cambodia listed the ring sport as Kun Khmer at the 2023 Games it hosted.

check.q: What does the 2023 name dispute show?

check.why: The dispute over Kun Khmer and muay showed that a name can carry national pride.

lessons.title: Muaythai and the Olympic Movement
lessons.mainIdea: The International Federation of Muaythai Associations gained full IOC recognition in 2021, a step toward the Olympic program.
reading: Muay Thai spread far beyond Thailand in the late 1900s. Gyms opened in Japan, the Netherlands, Britain, Australia and the United States. The 2003 Thai film Ong-Bak, starring Tony Jaa, drew new fans around the world. Many foreign fans travel to train at camps in Thailand.

Amateur Muay Thai needed a world *federation*, a group that joins national bodies and writes shared rules. The International Federation of Muaythai Associations, called *IFMA*, was founded in 1993. Its amateur rules call for safety gear that professional stadium bouts do not use. It spells the sport's name as one word, muaythai.

The International Olympic Committee, or IOC, gave IFMA provisional *recognition* in 2016. In 2021 it gave full recognition. Recognition means the IOC accepts the federation as the world body for the sport. It does not by itself put the sport on the Olympic program. Each Olympic Games still chooses its own list of sports.

the International Federation of Muaythai Associations, the world body for amateur Muay Thai

chapters.title: Silat, Arnis, a Chicago Gym
chapters.bigQuestion: When a martial art travels from a village to a school gym across the ocean, what changes and what stays the same?

story.title: Sticks on a Closet Shelf
story.kicker: A bundle of rattan sticks in a school closet leads back to the Philippines.
paragraphs: A PE teacher at a Chicago middle school opens the equipment closet. Next to the basketballs sits a bundle of rattan sticks. Each is about as long as an arm. The ends are wrapped in tape, and a label reads "arnis."

A student named Joel picks one up. His family came from Cebu, an island in the Philippines. "My uncle has sticks like this," he says. "He goes to a club on the North Side on Saturdays." The teacher tells him the sticks came with a unit a visiting instructor taught last spring.

Joel looks at the tape and the label. "In the Philippines, it is in the law," he says. "My uncle says arnis is the national martial art." The teacher looks it up on her phone. Joel is right. A law passed in 2009 named arnis the national martial art and sport of the Philippines.

Another student asks if the sticks are the same as the ones used long ago. The teacher is not sure. Rattan is a vine-like palm that grows in Southeast Asia, and it has been used for sticks for a long time. But a school unit with tape and a label is new.

Joel sets the stick back on the shelf. "So is this the real thing," he asks, "or is my uncle's club the real thing?" The teacher says it is a good question for history class. Both the club and the closet have a story.
story.think: Can a martial art be real in a school gym and also real at a family festival? Why or why not?

lessons.title: One Word, Many Arts
lessons.mainIdea: Silat is a family of martial arts practiced across the Malay world, from Indonesia and Malaysia to Brunei, Singapore, southern Thailand and the southern Philippines.
reading: *Silat* is not one single art. It is a family of many arts with shared roots. People practice it in Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore. It is also practiced in southern Thailand and the southern Philippines, where many Malay and Muslim communities live.

In Indonesia, the common name is *pencak silat*. Some teachers use pencak for the art's movement and display, and silat for its use in defense. Each region has its own styles. In West Sumatra, the Minangkabau people call their art silek. In West Java, the name Cimande comes from a village and river where a well-known style grew.

Hundreds of named silat schools exist today. Each one has its own teachers and its own line of students. Because the family is so large, historians avoid saying silat began at one place or one date. They trace many local roots instead.

words.d: a family of martial arts practiced across the Malay world of Southeast Asia
the common Indonesian name for the silat arts
a people of West Sumatra, Indonesia, whose silat is called silek

check.why: The Minangkabau people of West Sumatra call their art silek.

lessons.title: Silat at Weddings and Festivals
lessons.mainIdea: In many communities, silat is performed with music at weddings, festivals and ceremonies, not only practiced as self-defense.
reading: In many Malay communities, silat is part of a *wedding*. A silat performer may lead the bride and groom forward as drums play. The drums are often the gendang, a two-headed drum. Guests watch the display as a sign of respect and welcome.

Silat is also performed at harvest festivals, national holidays and the opening of important events. In these settings, the display is an *art form*, judged by its grace and its link to the music. Performers wear traditional clothing, often with a sarong or a folded headcloth.

Some silat schools grew around villages, prayer houses or family lines. Teaching often took place at night or after work. Students learned from one teacher over many years. These community roles are older than any sport rule book, and they continue today.

words.d: a marriage ceremony; in many Malay communities, silat is performed there to honor the couple
a practice valued for its beauty and meaning, not only its use
a two-headed drum played in Malay and Indonesian music, including at silat displays

lessons.title: From IPSI to PERSILAT
lessons.mainIdea: Indonesia founded a national pencak silat body, IPSI, in 1948, and four countries founded the world body, PERSILAT, in 1980.
reading: Indonesia declared independence in 1945. The new nation wanted national symbols. In 1948, Indonesians founded *IPSI*, the Indonesian Pencak Silat Association, in the city of Surakarta. IPSI worked to bring many silat schools under one national body.

In 1980, four countries founded *PERSILAT*, the International Pencak Silat Federation, in Jakarta. The four were Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei. PERSILAT wrote shared rules so athletes from different countries could meet. Many more countries have joined since.

Shared rules made silat a *regional* sport. Pencak silat joined the Southeast Asian Games in 1987, when Jakarta hosted. National bodies choose athletes and send them to these events. Village teachers and national federations now work side by side.

words.d: the Indonesian Pencak Silat Association, founded in 1948
the International Pencak Silat Federation, founded in Jakarta in 1980
shared across a group of nearby countries

lessons.title: Match and Art Events
lessons.mainIdea: Sport pencak silat has two kinds of events: tanding, a scored match, and seni, an artistic event judged on set routines.
reading: Sport pencak silat under PERSILAT rules has two main kinds of events. The first is *tanding*, a scored match between two athletes. Athletes are grouped by sex and by weight. Judges score each round.

The second is *seni*, which means art. In seni events, athletes perform set routines, and judges score them. There are events for one person, called tunggal, for two people, called ganda, and for teams of three, called regu. Some routines are performed with traditional weapons such as a staff or a short blade.

Having both kinds of events keeps two sides of silat in the rule book. Tanding looks like other combat sports, with rounds and weight classes. Seni keeps the display side seen at festivals. Many countries send athletes to both.

lessons.title: Asian Games and UNESCO
lessons.mainIdea: In 2018 pencak silat appeared at the Asian Games in Indonesia, and in 2019 UNESCO listed silat traditions from both Indonesia and Malaysia.
reading: The *Asian Games* are a large multi-sport event held every four years for countries across Asia. In 2018, Indonesia hosted them in Jakarta and Palembang. As host, Indonesia added pencak silat to the program. Indonesian athletes won most of the pencak silat gold medals.

UNESCO is the United Nations group for education, science and culture. It keeps a list of *intangible cultural heritage*. That means living traditions, such as music, crafts and ceremonies, rather than buildings. Countries ask UNESCO to add their traditions to the list.

In December 2019, UNESCO added two entries. One was the Traditions of Pencak Silat, from Indonesia. The other was Silat, from Malaysia. Both countries were honored in the same year. The two entries show that one family of arts can be claimed with pride by more than one nation.

words.d: a multi-sport event held every four years for countries across Asia
the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization
living traditions such as music, crafts and ceremonies, listed by UNESCO

check.why: Indonesia hosted the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta and Palembang and added pencak silat.

check.why: Intangible cultural heritage means living traditions, not buildings.

lessons.title: Names Borrowed From Spanish
lessons.mainIdea: The Filipino stick-based arts go by several names, and two of them, arnis and eskrima, come from Spanish words.
reading: The Philippines has a family of martial arts known for sticks and blades. People call them by several names. The best known are *arnis*, *eskrima* and kali. In many clubs, the names are used almost as if they mean the same thing.

Two of these names come from Spanish. Spain ruled the Philippines from the 1500s until 1898. The word arnis likely comes from the Spanish arnés, meaning armor or harness. The word eskrima comes from the Spanish esgrima, meaning fencing.

The origin of the name kali is debated. Some teachers link it to older Filipino words. Historians say the evidence is thin. What is clear is that the arts belong to many islands and languages, such as Cebuano, Ilocano and Tagalog. Each region kept its own teachers and styles.

words.d: a Filipino martial art known for sticks and blades; the name likely comes from Spanish arnés
another name for the Filipino stick arts, from Spanish esgrima, meaning fencing
a vine-like palm of Southeast Asia, used to make arnis sticks

look.prompt: What do these borrowed names tell you about the history of the Philippines?

check.why: Spain ruled the Philippines from the 1500s until 1898.

lessons.title: Mactan, 1521, and the Stories After
lessons.mainIdea: Lapulapu's forces defeated Ferdinand Magellan at Mactan in 1521; later claims that they used arnis are a proud story, not a documented fact.
reading: In April 1521, the Portuguese sailor Ferdinand Magellan, leading a Spanish fleet, landed on the island of Mactan. Its chief, *Lapulapu*, refused to submit. In the fight that followed, Magellan was killed. Lapulapu is honored today as a Filipino hero.

Our main record of the battle comes from Antonio *Pigafetta*. He was an Italian who sailed with Magellan and kept a journal. He wrote that the fighters of Mactan used spears, shields and blades, and that there were very many of them. He does not name any martial art.

Many arnis teachers today say that Lapulapu's fighters practiced an early form of their art. This is a proud story. Historians note that no record from 1521 names such an art. The story is best held as tradition, beside the journal as evidence.

words.d: the chief of Mactan whose forces defeated Magellan in 1521
Antonio Pigafetta, an Italian who sailed with Magellan and wrote the main account of the voyage

look.prompt: What does Pigafetta tell us about the fighters of Mactan? What does he not tell us?

check.why: Lapulapu, the chief of Mactan, led the forces that defeated Magellan.

check.q: Who wrote the main account of the battle at Mactan?
check.why: Antonio Pigafetta, who sailed with Magellan, kept the main journal of the voyage.

choices: No record from 1521 names such an art.

check.why: No record from 1521 names arnis, so the claim is a proud tradition, not a documented fact.

lessons.title: A National Martial Art by Law
lessons.mainIdea: Republic Act No. 9850, signed in 2009, made arnis the national martial art and sport of the Philippines.
reading: In 2009, the Philippine Congress passed *Republic Act No. 9850*. President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo signed it in December of that year. The law declared arnis the *national martial art* and sport of the Philippines.

The law named the Philippine Sports Commission as the lead agency for arnis. It also called for arnis to be promoted in schools and national sports events. Since then, many Filipino schoolchildren meet arnis in physical education classes.

A national law is a strong kind of recognition. It turns a family of local arts into a symbol of the whole country. Some older teachers welcomed this. Others worried that one official version might crowd out the many island styles.

words.d: the 2009 Philippine law that made arnis the national martial art and sport
a martial art a country officially names as a symbol of the nation
the government body for sports in the Philippines

look.prompt: What is each teacher hopeful or worried about? Can both be right?

lessons.title: Arnis as a Sport
lessons.mainIdea: Sport arnis uses padded sticks, protective gear and scoring rules, and it first appeared at the Southeast Asian Games in 2005.
reading: In the later 1900s, arnis groups began to hold more scored matches. To make matches safer, groups added *protective gear*, such as padded vests and helmets with face cages. Some rules use sticks covered in foam padding. Referees and judges score each round.

Different groups wrote different rule books. The World Eskrima Kali Arnis Federation, called *WEKAF*, was founded in Cebu in the late 1980s. It holds world championships with athletes from many countries. Other groups in the Philippines keep their own rules.

Arnis first appeared at the Southeast Asian Games in 2005, when the Philippines hosted. Sport events include scored matches and events judged on set routines. Many clubs call a routine *anyo*. Like silat, arnis keeps both a match side and a display side.

words.d: padded vests, helmets and other equipment worn to make matches safer
the World Eskrima Kali Arnis Federation, founded in Cebu in the late 1980s
a set routine performed and judged in sport arnis

lessons.title: Laws That Shaped Filipino Migration
lessons.mainIdea: U.S. laws in 1903, 1934, 1946 and 1965 opened and closed the door for Filipinos coming to the United States.
reading: The United States took control of the Philippines from Spain in 1898, after the Spanish-American War. In 1903, the U.S.-run government of the islands created the *pensionado* program. It sent Filipino students to study at American colleges, including schools in the Midwest.

In the 1920s, many Filipino men came to work on farms in California and Hawaii and in cities such as Chicago. The Tydings-McDuffie Act of 1934 promised the Philippines independence. It also cut Filipino immigration to 50 people a year. The Luce-Celler Act of 1946 let Filipino immigrants become U.S. citizens. The Philippines became independent that same year.

The *Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965* ended the old quota system based on national origin. After it, many more Filipino families came to the United States. Many were nurses, doctors and engineers. They brought their arts, foods and languages with them, including arnis.

words.d: a Filipino student sent to study in the United States under a program begun in 1903
a limit on how many people from a country may immigrate each year
the U.S. law that ended immigration quotas based on national origin

lessons.title: Stockton, Chicago and Community Clubs
lessons.mainIdea: Filipino communities in Stockton, Chicago and other cities kept eskrima alive in family backyards and community clubs before it reached public classes.
reading: Stockton, California, had one of the largest Filipino communities in the United States in the early 1900s. Its downtown area was known as Little Manila. Farm workers from the Philippines taught eskrima to one another in backyards and halls. For years, many teachers taught only Filipino students.

In the 1960s, Stockton teachers began to open their classes to the public. *Angel Cabales* is often named as one of the first to run an eskrima school open to anyone. Students from many backgrounds came. Some of them later became well-known teachers themselves.

Chicago also has a long Filipino history. Pensionado students studied in the Midwest after 1903. In the 1920s and 1930s, many Filipino men in Chicago worked for the *Pullman Company*, which ran sleeping cars on the railroads. Later, many Filipino nurses came to Chicago hospitals. Community groups and clubs grew with the population, and some taught arnis.

lessons.title: Gym and Festival, Both Real
lessons.mainIdea: When silat and arnis travel, they live in both sport gyms and community gatherings, and each setting is a real part of the tradition.
reading: Silat also traveled. After the Netherlands recognized Indonesia's independence in 1949, many Indo families, of mixed Dutch and Indonesian descent, moved to the Netherlands. Some brought pencak silat with them. Silat clubs grew in Dutch cities and later spread across Europe.

In a new country, an art often lives in two places. One is the sport gym, with rules, weight classes, scoring and a national federation. The other is the community gathering, where the art is shown at weddings, holidays and family events. Both places have teachers who learned from older teachers.

It can be tempting to call one version real and the other fake. Historians of the *diaspora* see it differently. A school unit, a Saturday club and a village festival are all part of the art's history. Each setting keeps some parts and changes others.

The Tydings-McDuffie Act set a quota of 50.
review.why: The 1965 law ended the old quota system, and many more Filipino families came.

review.q: What did UNESCO do in December 2019?
choices: listed silat traditions from both Indonesia and Malaysia
review.why: UNESCO listed the Traditions of Pencak Silat (Indonesia) and Silat (Malaysia) in December 2019.

review.q: In what setting is silat often performed with gendang drums to honor a couple?
review.why: In many Malay communities, silat is performed at weddings with drums such as the gendang.
